![](../../src/images/hex_complex.png){.intro_image fig-alt="Course logo"}

Objects in R can be thought of as containers that store information. There are three general categories of objects that we typically use in R:

-   **Functions** contain a series of commands used to complete a given task.
-   **Environments** are unordered collections of names with bindings to other objects.
-   **Data objects** organize values or component objects in an ordered, predictable way.

In this lesson, we will begin our exploration of each of these types of objects. In doing so, I will introduce a lot of the terminology that we will use throughout this course (pay close attention to **bold text**!). You will learn:

* What a function is (and what is not a function)
* Prefix vs. infix functions
* What the term "Global Environment" means and how to manage it effectively
* How package namespaces and attached package environments differ, and how to access package contents with `::` or `library()`
* The most common data objects (atomic vectors, matrices, lists, and data frames) and how they are related

::: {.callout-important}

This lesson assumes that you have completed the preliminary lessons. As the material covered herein will build on the content in those lessons, please do not proceed until their completion.

:::

</div>

## Before you begin

To get the most out of this lesson, please:

* Open RStudio in a clean session.
* Ensure that you are working in your course project.
* Open the script file `scripts/lesson_1.3.R`.
* Code along with the content!

## Functions

A **function** is a set of instructions used to complete a given task. Ultimately, anything that happens is the result of running a function ([John Chambers, userR!2014](http://user2014.r-project.org/files/chambers.pdf){target="_blank"}). Early in the R learning process, R seems to be an endless, and often overwhelming, collection of functions. The R learner is typically engaged with how to complete the tasks before them (e.g., statistical analyses) and finds themselves slowly gathering a series of functions that will become the foundation of their R toolkit. A side effect of this process is that it leaves the false impression that developing R skills *is* the process of adding functions to that toolkit. Learning new functions is certainly a part of learning R, but I would argue that it is far from the most important component (which I believe is understanding the language ... *why* things work the way they do).

Most functions are called with:

* A name: R evaluates the name and follows its binding to retrieve the function object
* Parentheses: Parentheses instruct R to run a function based on the arguments within the parentheses
* Argument(s): The data upon which the function will act

### Prefix functions

The majority of functions in R are known as **prefix functions**. A prefix function is a function in which the name of the function precedes the target of the evaluation. To run most prefix functions, you supply the name assigned to the set of instructions, a set of parentheses, and the target of evaluation. Consider the following code:

```{r}
c(1, 1, 2, 3)
```

In the above:

* The name `c` is bound to the combine function and is used to retrieve it;
* The parentheses tell R to execute the function using the arguments that are enclosed within the parentheses;
* The values inside the parentheses are the target of the execution;
* Each argument is separated by a comma.

**Prefix operators**: A few prefix functions are **operators** (but not many!). Operators are functions that are referenced by a symbol and do not require parentheses to specify the target of evaluation. Examples of prefix operators are the help operator (`?`), the negative symbol (`-`, when used to specify a negative number), and the "not" symbol (`!`):

```{r}
#| eval: false

?TRUE

-TRUE

!TRUE
```

::: mysecret
{{< fa screwdriver-wrench size=2x >}} [Not all symbols are operators!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

It is important to recognize that *some* symbols are operators and *all* operators are functions. It is equally important, however, to recognize that **not all symbols are operators**. There are a number of symbols in R that carry a special meaning but are not functions in and of themselves. These include, but are not limited to, commas (`x, y`), single quotation marks (`'x'`), double quotation marks (`"x"`), and backticks (`` `x` ``).
:::

### Infix functions

An **infix function** is a function in which the name of the function is placed between the function's arguments. Most of the operators that we use in R are infix functions. We learned examples of several infix operators in the preliminary lessons, which include (but are not limited to):

* Assignment operators: `<-` and `=`;
* Mathematical operators, such as `+`, `/`, and `*`;
* Logical operators, such as `==`, `>`, and `%in%`;
* The sequence operator (`:`) and namespace operator (`::`);
* The `$` extraction operator.

### Square brackets

Square bracket operators (`[...]`, `[..., ...]`, and `[[...]]`) *are* functions, but their usual syntax is neither prefix nor infix. Instead, they enclose expressions or indices and must include an opening bracket and a paired closing bracket.

### Primitive functions

The base R distribution includes access to **primitive functions**, which call code written in C and are made available when we start a session.

Primitive functions may use prefix or infix syntax. Some are invoked with other forms of special syntax, including grouping parentheses (`(...)`), braces (`{...}`), and square brackets (`[...]` and `[[...]]`). Examples of primitive prefix functions include `c()`, `class()`, `list()`, and `rep()`. Most prefix and infix operators are primitive functions.

You can see whether a function is primitive or an R function in your console by wrapping its name in backticks and pressing Enter:

```{r}
`<-`
```

### Getting help with functions

It is *super* important to read the help file with functions that you are not familiar with! As we covered in the preliminary content, you can access the help file for most functions by supplying the `?` prefix operator followed by the name of the function:

```{r}
#| eval: false

?c
```

For operators, you must wrap the function inside of backtick quotes:

```{r}
#| eval: false

?`<-`
```

::: mysecret
{{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Functions change and so do we!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

Regularly re-reading help files for functions that you are familiar with is important. The arguments of functions are often updated with new versions of packages. Moreover, as our familiarity with a function increases over time, so does our ability to read and understand the function's usage.
:::

*Note: We will soon be writing our own custom functions ... but not today!*

```{r}
#| include: false

.function_exercise_helpers <- new.env(parent = globalenv())

sys.source(
  "src/r/course_functions.R",
  envir = .function_exercise_helpers
)
```

## Environments

In R, an **environment** can be thought of as an unordered collection of names with **bindings** to objects in memory. An environment stores the names and their bindings, not the objects themselves. That sounds simple enough, but there is a bit of computer jargon that we should unpack:

-   What is **memory**? Memory, or more specifically random access memory (RAM), is a temporary storage location for instructions (functions) and data. Memory allows for fast processing times (as opposed to data stored on a hard drive) because it is stored in a location that is very close to your computer's processor.
-   What is a **name**? A name is a symbol that R can evaluate to retrieve an object.
-   What is a **binding**? A binding is the association between a name in an environment and an object in memory. **Assignment** creates or changes a binding.

In his book [Advanced R](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/){target="_blank"}, Hadley Wickham calls an environment a "bag of names" — that is a helpful way to remember that environments store names rather than the objects themselves.

### The global environment

Whenever you use R, you are working in an environment. The environment we work in the most is known as the **global environment**. It contains the names and bindings that we create there during the current session.

We can view the names in the global environment with the function `ls()`:

```{r}
ls()
```

Our global environment is currently empty. When we assign an object to a name at the console, R typically creates a binding for that name in the global environment. The object exists in memory, and evaluating the name follows the binding to retrieve the object.

```{r}
greetings <- "hello world"

ls()
```

We can then retrieve the object simply by evaluating the name stored in our global environment:

```{r}
greetings
```

<!-- Here is where I moved the typical setup -->

```{r}
#| include: false

source("src/r/course_functions.R")

```

### Package namespaces and attached package environments

R packages use several environments. Two are especially important for our work:

* A package's **namespace** contains the package's functions and other objects, including both exported objects intended for users and internal objects used by the package. A namespace is loaded when the package's code is needed, even if the package is not attached.
* An **attached package environment** contains bindings to the package's exported objects and appears on R's search path after we call `library()`.

```{r}
#| include: false

if ("package:tibble" %in% search()) {
  detach(
    "package:tibble",
    unload = FALSE,
    character.only = TRUE
  )
}

if ("package:tidyverse" %in% search()) {
  detach(
    "package:tidyverse",
    unload = FALSE,
    character.only = TRUE
  )
}
```

When we open a clean R session, the global environment and several package environments from the base R distribution (e.g., *stats* and *utils*) are already on the search path. We can view the search path with `search()`:

```{r}
search()
```

The result shows the environments in which R looks for an unqualified name. It does not list every namespace that is loaded. We can view those with `loadedNamespaces()`.

Installing a package (e.g., with `install.packages("tidyverse")`) saves its contents to your hard drive, but it does not attach the package environment to the current R session.

For example, the function `tribble()` is exported by the *tibble* package. We downloaded that package when we installed the *tidyverse* metapackage. If *tibble* is installed but not attached, R cannot find the unqualified name `tribble` on its search path:

```{r}
#| eval: false

tribble(
  ~ a, ~ b,
    1,   1,
    2,   3
)
```

In a session where *tibble* is installed but not attached, this call produces:

```text
Error: could not find function "tribble"
```

We can retrieve an exported object directly from a package namespace with the `::` operator. If necessary, `::` loads the namespace, but it does not attach the package environment:

```{r}
tibble::tribble(
  ~ a, ~ b,
    1,   1,
    2,   3
)
```

The expression above retrieves the `tribble` function object from the *tibble* namespace. The package environment is still not on the search path. Calling `tribble()` without `tibble::` would produce the same error.

Using `::` is useful when you call only a few functions from a package or want to make the source of a function explicit. It also avoids ambiguity when multiple packages export the same name.

An alternative is to attach the package environment with `library()`. Calling `library()` loads the namespace if necessary and adds the package's attached environment to the search path. This approach is useful when a script repeatedly uses functions from the package:

```{r}
#| message: false

library(tibble)
```

We can now call the function without the use of the `::` operator:

```{r}
tribble(
  ~ a, ~ b,
    1,   1,
    2,   3
)
```

The above now works because `library()` added the attached *tibble* environment to R's search path for the current session. Run `search()` again to confirm that `"package:tibble"` now appears.

::: mysecret
{{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Do not individually attach core tidyverse packages!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

I do not typically attach *tibble* with `library(tibble)`. The *tibble* package is one of the **core tidyverse packages**, which are a subset of tidyverse packages that may be attached with:

```{r}
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
```

Because I use functions from multiple core tidyverse packages in almost every R session, it does not make sense to attach the package environments individually.

To produce a character vector of *all* of the packages in the tidyverse (both core and non-core), run the following code:

```{r}
tidyverse_packages()
```

To see which core tidyverse package environments were attached, run `search()` after calling `library(tidyverse)`.

*Note: Core tidyverse packages also import functions from other tidyverse packages. For example, the tibble package imports some (but not all) functions from magrittr, pillar, and rlang.*
:::

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Check your understanding]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

Which statement best describes what happens when you call `tibble::tribble()` before attaching *tibble*?

`r longmcq(c("R attaches the tibble package environment to the search path", answer = "R loads the tibble namespace if necessary and retrieves its exported tribble function without attaching the package environment", "R copies the tribble function into the global environment", "R installs the tibble package from CRAN"))`
:::

### Community packages

The R community has generated thousands of packages for a variety of applications. Many of these packages have changed the way that we code in R (e.g., the *tidyverse* family of packages) and greatly expanded what we can use R to do. Through this awesome community of coders, we can now use R to process and visualize geospatial data, make professional-looking websites, perform advanced image processing, and even retrieve our local weather forecast — the sky is the limit, and it is all free! Using community packages is (and should be) a regular part of our R workflow, but I strongly suggest avoiding what I call "package hunting" ...

::: mysecret
{{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Don't be a package hunter!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

We've all been there — we encounter a problem that we cannot figure out how to solve, visit Stack Overflow, discover that "there's a package for that!", install the package, and repeat. Before we know it, the tops of our scripts are cluttered with ten `library()` calls, many of which may be unnecessary.

The decision to install or use a package should be made carefully:

* Ask whether it is necessary — does it add functionality that is not available in the packages you already use?
* Consider its documentation, testing, source, and adoption by the relevant community.
* Review its maintenance history and unresolved issues. A mature, stable package may not require frequent updates, but abandoned packages can create reproducibility and compatibility problems.
* Decide whether its limitations are acceptable for your work — packages often simplify a task but may impose strict behavior that does not suit your specific use case.

As a final warning, no package should be trusted outright — validate package behavior whenever an error could affect your analysis. For example, I used a very popular package (that shall remain unnamed) during my dissertation. I found an error in one of its functions only after spending days reviewing its code and cited papers. Dozens of peer-reviewed studies have used that function.
:::

```{r}

source("src/r/reference_lookup.R")
lesson_refs <- find_lesson_references()
```

## Data objects

In this course, I will use the term **data objects** to describe objects that organize values or component objects in an ordered structure.

The **order** of a data object allows us to reference values by position (unlike environments, which are unordered). Consider, for example, the following numeric vector:

```{r}
c(1, 1, 2, 3)
```

The value "2" in the above vector is the third value in the vector. Because the data are ordered, we can index the vector with the `[[...]]` function to extract the value at the third position:

```{r}
c(1, 1, 2, 3)[[3]]
```

The **structure** of a data object primarily describes the **dimensionality** of the enclosing container (typically in one or two dimensions) and whether its underlying values or components are **homogeneous** (one type) or **heterogeneous** (more than one type).

The primary classes of objects that we will work with in this course are atomic vectors, lists, matrices, and data frames. These classes determine *how* we work with them.

The table below may help you sort between the structure of these common data objects:

|                      | Homogeneous    | Heterogeneous  |
|:--------------------:|:--------------:| --------------:|
| **One-dimensional**  | Atomic vector  | List           |
| **Two-dimensional**  | Matrix         | Data frame     |

The above is a handy (and often used) way to describe the structure of different object classes. However, I have found that it can lead to some confusion when working with these data objects. In an attempt to avoid this we will look at:

* **Class**: How R interprets an object and, for generic functions, which methods R may use with it. We will assess this with `class()`.
* **Type**: The object's underlying storage type. We will assess this with `typeof()`.

::: mysecret
{{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Evaluate the class and type of every data object that you create or use!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}
:::

### Atomic vectors

An **atomic vector** is a one-dimensional object in which every value has the same underlying type. Class applies to the vector as a whole rather than independently to each value.

We can generate an atomic vector using the combine function, `c()`, and assign it to the name `my_numbers`:

```{r}
my_numbers <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)

my_numbers
```

We can determine the class of the vector with `class()`:

```{r}
class(my_numbers)
```

The above is not surprising; we have supplied numeric values and thus created a numeric vector.

The type of an atomic vector, however, is not always straightforward. The numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4 are **integers** (i.e., whole numbers), so it seems that `my_numbers` should be stored as integer values, right? Let's see:

```{r}
typeof(my_numbers)
```

It is not! It is a **double numeric vector**. Double precision is R's default storage type for numeric values, including values that happen to be whole numbers.

To create an integer vector with adjacent numbers, we can use the sequence operator (`:`):

```{r}
typeof(1:4)
```

What if the numbers are non-adjacent? When the values are already whole numbers, we can convert a double vector to integer type with `as.integer()`. Likewise, we can use `as.numeric()` to transform an integer vector to double type.

Conversion between atomic vector classes and types can sometimes pose challenges. For example, let's create an atomic character vector and assign the object to a name (with the assignment function, `<-`):

```{r}
musicians <-
  c(
    "roger",
    "pete",
    "john",
    "keith"
  )

class(musicians)
```

*Note: `musicians` is a name bound to the character vector. Evaluating the name retrieves that object.*

Let's see what happens if we try to convert this character vector to numeric:

```{r}
#| warning: true

as.numeric(musicians)
```

We get a warning message! The values were converted to `NA` because R had no way of knowing how to describe the values numerically.

Conversely, recall that factor vectors have an underlying integer type. We can convert our musicians from characters to factors with `factor()`:

```{r}
musician_factor <- factor(musicians)

musician_factor
```

We can then observe its underlying type:

```{r}
typeof(musician_factor)
```

Because the factor has integer type, `as.numeric()` returns its internal integer codes. The expression runs, but it does **not** convert the displayed labels into meaningful numeric values:

```{r}
as.numeric(musician_factor)
```

You should therefore avoid using `as.numeric()` directly on a factor when you intend to convert its labels. To see what the codes represent, we can inspect the factor's structure with `str()`:

```{r}
str(musician_factor)
```

In the above, we can see the class of the object (factor), its levels, and the integer codes that make up the vector. By default, factor levels are usually sorted alphanumerically according to the current locale.

::: mysecret
{{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [All values in an atomic vector must share the same type!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

Notice what happens when we use `c()` to combine two vectors of different classes:

```{r}
c(musicians, 1:4)
```

Because `c()` generates an atomic vector and all values in an atomic vector must share one underlying type, R coerced the integer values to character. Use `class()` or `typeof()` to confirm that the result is character. Knowing this can help identify problems in a data set. For example, if you read in a data set and a column that should be numeric has character type, a character value may be present somewhere in the column.
:::

### Matrices

A **matrix** is an atomic vector with an additional attribute that arranges the data as rows and columns (i.e., it is a two-dimensional object).

We can create a matrix from scratch using `matrix()`. We supply:

* An atomic vector of values
* The number of rows (`nrow = ...`) and/or columns (`ncol = ...`) to arrange the data into
* The order in which to populate the matrix (`byrow = FALSE` or `byrow = TRUE`)

```{r}
my_matrix <-
  matrix(
    1:4,
    nrow = 2,
    ncol = 2,
    byrow = TRUE
  )

my_matrix
```

The matrix was populated by row because we set `byrow = TRUE`. It should come as no surprise that the class of the data object is a matrix (we did just generate a matrix, after all):

```{r}
class(my_matrix)
```

... a peek under the hood, however, shows us that the data are stored as an atomic vector!

```{r}
typeof(my_matrix)
```

What we *have* done is add an attribute to the vector that describes its dimensions. We can investigate this with `attributes()`:

```{r}
attributes(my_matrix)
```

The `byrow` argument changes how the input vector is arranged into rows and columns, but R still stores the resulting matrix as a one-dimensional atomic vector with a dimension attribute.

::: mysecret
{{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [A matrix *is* an atomic vector (and that matters)!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

Because a matrix *is* an atomic vector (with an additional attribute defining dimensions), all values in a matrix must be atomic:

```{r}
matrix(
  c(musicians, 1:4),
  nrow = 4,
  ncol = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)
```

:::

### Lists

A list is a one-dimensional object (i.e., vector) where values, which I will call **list items**, can be of any class or type.

We can generate a list with the `list()` function. Let's combine our `musicians` and the integers `1:4` into a list and assign the name `my_list` to the data object:

```{r}
my_list <- list(musicians, 1:4)
```

Have a look at the values in the resulting object:

```{r}
my_list
```

The class and type of each component object were maintained because lists are not atomic. Instead, lists are **recursive objects** — data objects whose elements refer to component objects. Unlike an atomic vector, a list can therefore contain objects of different classes and types. For the object `my_list`, both `class()` and `typeof()` return `"list"`.

If we look at the structure of the data, we can see that the list is composed of two different atomic vectors (a character vector and an integer vector):

```{r}
str(my_list)
```

It is important to distinguish an environment binding from a list element. The global environment contains a binding from the name `my_list` to the list object in memory. The list object, in turn, contains two ordered elements that refer to component objects: a character vector and an integer vector. A list element is not an environment binding, even when the element has a name.

Because each list element can refer to a separate object, the list does not need to be atomic. In practice, this means that lists are very flexible to work with. However ...

::: mysecret
<i class="fas fa-user-secret" style="font-size:36px"></i>   [Restrictions are <strike>annoying</strike> great!]{style="font-size: 20px"}

The flexibility of lists makes them very powerful ... unfortunately, it can also make them difficult to work with and prone to errors. Restrictions in the behavior of objects make it much easier to spot problems in our data.
<br>
:::

### Data frames

A **data frame** is a restrictive class of list that is arranged in rows and columns. Each column in a data frame represents a list item. Data frames have three important restrictions that distinguish them from other lists:

-   Each column (i.e., variable) in a data frame is a vector, and all columns have the same length.
-   A column is usually an atomic vector with one underlying type, but it may instead be a list-column whose elements contain objects of different classes and types.
-   A name must be assigned to each column (if not, it will be assigned for you).

We can use the function `data.frame()` to combine two vectors into a data frame and assign the object to the name `my_df`:

```{r}
my_df <-
  data.frame(
    musician = musicians,
    number = 1:4
  )
```

... and have a look at the data:

```{r}
my_df
```

Printing the structure of the data frame reveals that it is a list-based object with two vector columns:

```{r}
str(my_df)
```

In the above, we can see that the data frame contains two variables (columns), each with four observations (rows), and that each variable is an atomic vector.

*Notice that the components of `my_df` are the columns, not the rows — that knowledge will serve you well in the coming lessons.*

::: mysecret
<i class="fas fa-user-secret" style="font-size:36px"></i>   [Variables and observations!]{style="font-size: 20px"}

Once we start to dive into the tidyverse, the terminology "variable" and "observation" become super important:

* **Variable**: A column in a data frame
* **Observation**: A row within a data frame
<br>
:::

Let's take a look at the class of the object and how it is stored. Note that the class of this object is data frame. Its type is list (i.e., the data are stored as a list)!

```{r}
class(my_df)

typeof(my_df)
```

### Tibble data frames

The above instance is the *only* time that we will use the function `data.frame()` in this course (personally, I never use it). Instead, we will use **tibble** data frames, which are a special, restrictive class of data frame.

To generate a tibble data frame, we can use the function `tibble()` to combine two vectors into a single data object:

```{r}
# A tibble of musicians and their instruments:

my_tibble <-
  tibble(
    musician = musicians,
    number = 1:4
  )

my_tibble
```

The most apparent difference between a tibble and a typical data frame is that structural information on the tibble is printed by default. The above includes its dimensions, variable names and classes, and values. The values are truncated if there are many rows or columns.

The differences do not stop there, though — tibbles are also more restrictive. For example, notice the kind of object that is returned when we use indexing to extract the second column in a data frame:

```{r}
my_df[ , 2]
```

It is an atomic vector! For a tibble, the class of object does not change (it is still a tibble):

```{r}
my_tibble[ , 2]
```

Tibbles are also more restrictive during construction. They will recycle a single value. A vector of another length generates an error:

```{r}
#| error: true

tibble(
  a = 1:2,
  b = 1:4
)
```

::: mysecret
<i class="fas fa-user-secret" style="font-size:36px"></i>   [Hurray! An error message!]{style="font-size: 20px"}

Error messages are annoying but incredibly useful — we need to find a place in our hearts to appreciate them. With restrictions on a function's usage or on the structure and composition of a data object, error messages stop us from making mistakes. When we generate an error message, it generally means that there is something that we do not understand about the data that we are using or the function that is causing the error.
:::

#### Another way of generating tibbles ...

It is often useful to use the `tribble()` function to generate a tibble. This allows for row-wise tibble construction — in other words, `tribble()` allows us to generate a tibble with code that looks like the output. To do so, each column name is preceded by the `~` operator and separated from the next specification by a comma. The `~` operator is a primitive function that constructs a formula; `tribble()` interprets each one-sided formula as a column specification. Values are then written in the positions that they will occupy in the resulting tibble.

```{r}
# Combining the two vectors into a tibble with tribble():

tribble(
  ~ musician, ~ number,
     "roger",        1,
      "pete",        2,
      "john",        3,
     "keith",        4
)
```

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Check your understanding]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

True or false: Every column in a data frame must be an atomic vector.

`r torf(FALSE)`
:::

## Indexing (enhanced review)

We explored indexing in ***Preliminary Lesson 5***. Given that the complexity of our code has increased at this point, it is worth revisiting some key elements of the indexing process, especially as it relates to data frames and tibbles.

Recall that we can extract an item from the list that we created earlier by position:

```{r}
my_list[[1]]
```

... or by name:

```{r}
names(my_list) <- c("musician", "number")

my_list[["musician"]]
```

Recall that a tibble is a restrictive type of data frame. A data frame is a restrictive type of list, and its columns (i.e., variables) are equivalent to the items in a list. As a result, we can extract a column from a data frame by position:

```{r}
my_tibble[[1]]
```

... or by name:

```{r}
my_tibble[["musician"]]
```

... which is equivalent to:

```{r}
my_tibble$musician
```

::: mysecret
{{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Avoid indexing by numeric indices!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

There are times when indexing by numeric indices is useful, especially during iteration, but this should typically be avoided when indexing columns. It is greatly preferred to extract by name rather than position because:

* It is much more communicative to let your readers (including your future self) know the variable that you are extracting or subsetting by.
* If the position of your columns has changed, you just broke your code!
:::

Of course, a data frame is a very special type of list — it has two dimensions! This gives us the power to index by row (observation), column (variable), or both:

```{r}
my_tibble[c(1, 4), ]

my_tibble[ , "musician"]

my_tibble[c(1, 4), "musician"]
```

This two-dimensional nature of a data frame gives us an incredible opportunity to use logic to subset data frames to rows that match a given condition or set of conditions.

Recall (from ***Preliminary Lesson 5***) that we can test whether the values in a vector match a given value using the `==` operator:

```{r}
my_tibble[["musician"]] == "roger"
```

... or test whether the values in a vector match a set of values using the `%in%` operator:

```{r}
my_tibble[["musician"]] %in% c("roger", "keith")
```

By nesting these statements within the row position of our two-dimensional indexing brackets (`[row, column]`), we can subset the data to rows in which our test evaluates to `TRUE`:

```{r}
my_tibble[
  my_tibble[["musician"]] == "roger", ]

my_tibble[
  my_tibble[["musician"]] %in% c("roger", "keith"), ]
```

Please note that I include the above predominantly to ensure that you have a strong understanding of the structure of data frame objects. In the real world, the above method tends to make our code very difficult to read, especially as our subsetting operations become more complex. We will soon use tidyverse methods for completing this in a way that is easier to read *and* write!

As a final aside ...

::: mysecret
{{< fa screwdriver-wrench size=2x >}} [What's the deal with `%in%` and why do I need it?]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

The use of `==` to subset a vector by a set of values is one of the biggest (and sometimes dangerous) mistakes that I see early R users make in their code. Let's take a moment to see why.

I will start by generating a vector of repeated fruits:

```{r}
my_vector <-
  rep(
    c("apple", "banana", "grape"),
    times = 2
  )

my_vector
```

Watch what happens when you evaluate the values based on a set of values:

```{r}
my_vector == c("apple", "banana")
```

Only the first two values evaluated to `TRUE`! Why? This occurs because the values in the second vector are recycled. R compares `"apple"` with `"apple"`, `"banana"` with `"banana"`, `"grape"` with `"apple"`, and so on. The logical test matches both the values and their positions. It does not check whether each value on the left occurs anywhere in the set on the right.

One option is to combine separate `==` comparisons with the *or* logical operator (`|`). As our queries become more complex, this quickly leads to messy code. As such, I *always* recommend using the base R operator `%in%` when comparing between sets!

```{r}
my_vector %in% c("apple", "banana")
```
:::

## Take-home points

* Functions may use prefix, infix, or other special syntax. Every operator is a function, including the `~` operator used to construct formulas.
* An environment stores names and bindings to objects in memory. A package namespace differs from an attached package environment, and `::` retrieves an exported object without attaching the package.
* Atomic vectors contain values of one underlying type. Matrices are atomic vectors with dimensions. Lists can contain component objects of different classes and types.
* Data frames are equal-length lists of columns, including possible list-columns. Prefer extracting columns by name, and use `%in%` when testing membership in a set of values.
